title: Surprise! The U.S. Added 172,000 Jobs in May—Here's What's Going On
summary: Did you hear the big news? The U.S. added 172,000 jobs in May! That's a lot more than economists thought would happen. They only expected about 110,000. It's the third month in a row of job gains. Kevin Hassett from the White House says the job market is "hitting on all cylinders." But wait—there's more to the story. Diane Swonk, a top economist, says a lot of those new jobs were in local government and in places like hotels and restaurants. That's partly because the World Cup is coming, and host cities are getting ready. The problem? Prices are still going up. Inflation might be over 4.2% soon. That means even though some people are earning more, many others feel like their money buys less. Swonk says the top third of earners are doing well, but the bottom two-thirds are losing ground. Also, some people can only find part-time work, and others have been jobless for a long time. So, the job market is a mixed bag: great for some, tough for others. It's like a puzzle where some pieces are bright and others are still cloudy.
why_it_matters: Even if job numbers sound good, half of the story is about rising prices, which might affect how your family budgets for snacks, school supplies, or summer trips.

background_read: Every month, the U.S. government counts how many new jobs were created; that number helps people know if the economy is strong.
The FIFA World Cup 2026 will be co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico, and host cities are already getting ready with new stadiums and hotels, creating temporary jobs.
When inflation rises, the same amount of money buys fewer groceries or gallons of gas, which is why some families feel poorer even if they have jobs.
Kevin Hassett (a White House economic advisor) says the job market is strong, while Diane Swonk (a top economist) points out that not everyone is winning.
Article_Structure: WHO: The U.S. government, economists Kevin Hassett and Diane Swonk, and American workers
WHAT: The U.S. added 172,000 jobs in May, beating expectations, but many jobs are part-time and inflation is hurting low-income earners
WHERE: In the United States, with host cities preparing for the World Cup
WHY: Job growth partly comes from World Cup preparation and local government hiring, but inflation and part-time work mean many Americans still struggle

perspectives.description: Kevin Hassett says the job market is strong and running well, with many new hires in hospitality and great overall numbers.
Swonk warns that mostly high earners are benefiting, while lower-income workers are losing ground because of inflation and part-time hours.
Job growth often happens unevenly; big events like the World Cup create temporary jobs that may disappear once the event is over.
